tagline: Mountain passes lead into a valley of old settlements and moving sand.
intro: Los Caminos Antiguos crosses the broad San Luis Valley between the Sangre de Cristo Range and the San Juan foothills. On Highway 17, Cumbres Pass reaches 10,022 feet, with a 5.8 percent northern approach. Beyond the mountains, the route links valley towns with the Great Sand Dunes. CDOT gives this Colorado Scenic and Historic Byway 129 miles and three hours of driving, emphasizing San Luis, Our Lady of Guadalupe parish and Fort Garland. The valley is a high-elevation basin averaging 7,664 feet above sea level, drained southward by the Rio Grande into New Mexico.

Road and railroad share Cumbres Pass, but their histories are distinct. The Denver & Rio Grande built its line over the pass in the early 1880s as part of the Alamosa-to-Durango San Juan Extension. Later highway realignment demolished some railroad structures, including the station. The original section house and part of the old snowshed remain at the pass.

Travel from the New Mexico border on Highway 17 toward Antonito and neighboring Conejos. Continue through Romeo and east on Highway 142 to San Luis, then north to Fort Garland. Highways 160 and 150 lead toward the dunes; the route then crosses through Mosca and turns south toward Alamosa East.

moments.title: Conejos
moments.text: Our Lady of Guadalupe in Conejos is Colorado’s oldest parish. Its history belongs to a settlement founded in 1858, when this was Taos County in New Mexico Territory. Colorado Territory followed in 1861, and the new county initially had its seat across the Conejos River at Guadalupe. Fear of flooding had already prompted the post office to move across the river in 1862 to ground three feet higher. The county seat moved to Conejos in 1863. Conejos remains an unincorporated county seat, immediately north of Antonito, with U.S. 285 along its eastern edge.

moments.title: San Luis
moments.text: San Luis’s Stations of the Cross climb a local mesa 250 feet high. Below them is Colorado’s oldest continuously occupied town, formerly called San Luis de la Culebra. Hispanic settlers from the Taos Valley established villages along the Rio Culebra and took possession of this part of the Sangre de Cristo Land Grant on April 9, 1851. The settlement remained in New Mexico Territory until Colorado Territory was created in 1861. The town celebrates the Fiesta de Santiago y Santa Ana in July and San Luis Manito Christmas in December.

moments.title: Fort Garland
moments.text: Fort Garland’s museum includes restored and reconstructed buildings, among them the adobe Commandant’s Quarters associated with Kit Carson and his wife. The Army post operated from 1858 to 1883. The Ninth U.S. Cavalry, known as Buffalo Soldiers, served here from 1876 to 1879. In 1877, those troops helped remove illegal white settlers from Ute reservation land. The Colorado Historical Society restored the fort and opened the museum in 1950. The cavalry barracks include exhibits of Hispanic traditional arts and nineteenth-century transportation. History Colorado administers the museum, whose permanent exhibits address Carson and the Buffalo Soldiers.

moments.title: Great Sand Dunes
moments.text: The Great Sand Dunes rise as high as 750 feet at the eastern edge of the San Luis Valley, below the Sangre de Cristo Range. Their sand came from sediments left exposed as lakes in the valley receded. Southwest winds carried it toward a low curve in the mountains; storm winds push back toward the valley, helping the dunes grow upward. Medano and Sand Creeks carry sand from the mountainside of the dune field back to the valley floor. There the creeks disappear into the sand sheet, and wind returns sand to the dunes.
